column1: # Performance budgets, and where each number comes from.
# The roadmap's Phase 0 appendix sets these; this file is where they stop being prose and start
# being a gate. A harness that emits numbers is a measurement, and a measurement nobody compares to
# a threshold is a number nobody reads -- which is the same shape as the evidence-nobody-consumes
# failure this project has now met five times.
# G5 is bytes, not milliseconds; its unit is named in the description because it is the one
# exception and hiding that in a column header would be worse than saying it here.
# G6 is bytes too, and it is a second budget rather than a bigger G5 on purpose. G5 bounds the
# HOST -- the WebAssembly modules, app.js and index.html, which a visitor downloads once and a
# browser then keeps behind an immutable content hash. G6 bounds the GUEST script, which is the
# Over-The-Air (OTA) payload and is re-fetched every time a product publishes. Folding the two
# together would make a payload change read as a client regression, and a kilobyte that is paid
# once per visitor would be averaged with a kilobyte that is paid once per visitor per release.
# G6 WAS ESTABLISHED AT 252,000 BYTES ON 2026-09-16, FROM A MEASUREMENT, NOT A GUESS.
# The measurement, on the distribution built by
# `./gradlew :samples:web-slice:wasmJsBrowserDistribution` at commit c424227:
#   guest-kotlin.js, brotli quality 11        243,951
#   guest-kotlin.js, uncompressed           1,223,843
# The ceiling is 252,000 -- 8,049 bytes of headroom, 3.30%, which is the proportion G5 carries
# (130,905 of 3,929,095, 3.33%) rounded to a number a person can hold in their head. Tight for the
# reason G5's is tight: on Fast 3G every 100 kilobytes is roughly half a second of waiting
# (ADR-038), and the guest is waited for on every release rather than once.
# This establishment is deliberately NOT an attribution, and the difference matters. There is no
# before-and-after here to attribute: the number is what the guest weighs today, measured for the
# first time. What it cannot say is what the generated Material 3 tier cost the guest, because the
# catalogue is not behind a build switch on the guest side the way the tier's registration is on
# the host side, so the three-build split G5 has could not be produced without changing product
# source. That is the gap being closed, stated rather than papered over: the tier grew the guest
# by an amount nobody measured, and from here nothing grows it unobserved.
# **From here, a raise to G6 obeys the same rule as a raise to G5**, below: three builds in the
# commit that makes it -- before the change, after it, and the split between whatever was added.
# A raise without one is a number nobody has to defend.
# 4.06 MB against a measured 3.93 MB: a ceiling with headroom rather than today's figure. Pinning it
# exactly fails on the next legitimate component and teaches everyone to raise the number, which is
# how a budget stops meaning anything. The headroom is deliberately tight -- about 130 kilobytes --
# because on Fast 3G every 100 kilobytes is roughly half a second of waiting (ADR-038).
# G5 WAS 3.90 MB, AND RAISING IT WAS AN OWNER DECISION (2026-09-16, ADR-072, OPEN-DECISIONS 7).
# The generated Material 3 tier -- 79 components, read from the library's own sources rather than
# hand-written -- was registered on the web profile. The attribution this rule demands, three
# builds of the web slice in brotli bytes:
#   without the tier at all                3,770,785
#   the tier linked but not registered     3,772,894   (+2,109)
#   the tier registered                    3,929,095   (+158,310)
# The 2,109 is the module merely being on the classpath, and it is the measurement that settles the
# engineering backlog's `D1`: dead-code elimination does drop an unregistered binding module. The
# 158,310 is what a payload's whole Material vocabulary costs every web client, globally, which is
# exactly the trade ADR-066 framed for the catalogue and is the reason the ceiling moves rather
# than the profile diverging. The alternative considered and rejected was leaving the tier out of
# the web build, which would have meant a payload could call `Button` on three clients and not in
# a browser.
# G5 WAS 3.70 MB, AND RAISING IT WAS AN OWNER DECISION, NOT A CONVENIENCE (2026-09-09, ADR-066).
# The catalogue grew from fourteen components to twenty and crossed the old ceiling. The decision
# taken was that a design system's components cost every web client their bytes, globally, the same
# way they cost every mobile client space in the installed binary -- so the two profiles stay
# aligned and the ceiling moves when the catalogue deliberately does.
# The obvious objection to that -- "then the number just keeps going up" -- is real, and this is
# what stops it being true silently:
#   **A raise to G5 must arrive with an attribution, in the commit that makes it.** Three builds:
#   before the change, after it, and the split between whatever components were added. That is what
#   turned "the bundle grew" into "the two Material 3 pickers cost 96,924 bytes and the other five
#   components cost 25,979 between them", which is a fact somebody can act on and a sentence
#   somebody can object to. A raise without one is a number nobody has to defend.
# The same rule, in one line, is in `docs/checks.md` beside the fixture-freezing rule, for the same
# reason: a rule that lives only in the file it governs is a rule found after it is broken.
# claim<TAB>budget<TAB>what it bounds
G1
